definition: Emaciated means extremely thin and wasted away, especially from lack of food.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word emaciated. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know emaciated should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Two winters in the prison camp had left the poet so emaciated that his own brother walked past him on the station platform.
Thin is neutral and often healthy — a thin distance runner is simply lean; thin stops far short of emaciated, which names dangerous wasting.
Gaunt is darker than thin — cheeks hollow, bones near the surface — but it still stops short of emaciated, the point where the body has plainly begun to waste away.

Skeletal means so thin that the bones stand out under the skin. It matches emaciated at the far end of thinness, but it names only the look: a frame can appear skeletal from any cause, while emaciated tells you the body has wasted, usually through hunger or illness.

Haggard describes a face worn out by exhaustion, worry, or strain — drawn features and shadowed eyes. You can look haggard after one sleepless week without losing a pound, while emaciated is about the body itself, thinned and hollowed by real hunger or disease.

Wasted describes flesh and muscle that hunger or disease has eaten away — doctors write of wasted limbs. It names the loss itself, while emaciated names the whole resulting look: a frame on which the loss is plain to see.

The workhouse inspector's 1842 report lingered on the children of the east ward: emaciated, their wrists no thicker than broom handles, they had been fed thin gruel for a year while the ledgers recorded meat.
Emaciated goes far beyond 'thin' or 'slender' — it names a body that has visibly wasted away, usually from starvation or illness.
A runner is lean by training; an emaciated child has been hollowed out by hunger.
Reach for emaciated only when a body has truly wasted — famine, illness, neglect; it belongs in doctors' notes and war reporting, and it turns insulting if aimed at someone merely slim.
For ordinary thinness, say thin, lean, or slender.
Its unit-mate enervated empties the batteries for an afternoon; emaciated empties the flesh itself.

The eagle came into the raptor center in late February, found grounded in a snowfield by a county plow driver.
Lead poisoning had kept it from hunting for weeks, and the bird was emaciated: under all those feathers, its breast muscle had shrunk to almost nothing and its keel stood out like a blade.
Feathers hide starvation well, the director explained; a bird can look full-bodied on a perch and still be hollowed out beneath.
The staff fed it in tiny, careful portions, since a body that has been starving too long can be killed by a sudden feast.
By May the eagle had rebuilt what the winter had taken, and the center released it on a ridge above the river.
